Two bugs. `otherPart` can be any part: a hat's Handle (whose parent is an Accessory, not the character), a dropped tool, or a loose brick, so `otherPart.Parent.Humanoid` errors. And `Touched` fires for every touching body part, many times per second, so one step deals 20 damage dozens of times. Resolve the character safely with `FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")` and `FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")`, and give each character a cooldown.

```lua
--!strict
-- Script inside the spike part
local spike = script.Parent :: BasePart

local DAMAGE = 20
local COOLDOWN = 1

local lastHit: { [Model]: number } = {}

local function characterFrom(hit: BasePart): (Model?, Humanoid?)
	local model = hit:FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")
	while model do
		local humanoid = model:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
		if humanoid then
			return model, humanoid
		end
		model = model:FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")
	end
	return nil, nil
end

spike.Touched:Connect(function(hit: BasePart)
	local character, humanoid = characterFrom(hit)
	if character == nil or humanoid == nil or humanoid.Health <= 0 then
		return
	end
	local now = os.clock()
	local last = lastHit[character]
	if last and now - last < COOLDOWN then
		return -- per-character cooldown: one hit per second however many parts touch
	end
	if last == nil then
		character.Destroying:Once(function()
			lastHit[character] = nil
		end)
	end
	lastHit[character] = now
	humanoid:TakeDamage(DAMAGE)
end)
```

- Walking up through ancestor Models handles parts nested inside accessories or tools held by the character.
- The cooldown table is keyed by character and cleared on `Destroying`, so it does not grow with every respawn.
- `TakeDamage` respects ForceFields (fresh spawns are safe); setting `Health` directly would not.

Event handlers each run in their own thread. `task.wait(1)` only pauses that one thread; Heartbeat still fires next frame and starts a new handler, so damage happens every frame (60 per second) and about 60 sleeping threads pile up at any time. Never yield to throttle a per-frame event: accumulate `dt` and act when a full interval has passed, or run a separate loop with `task.wait`.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.LavaDamage
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local INTERVAL = 1
local DAMAGE = 10

local LavaDamage = {}

function LavaDamage.tick()
	for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
		local character = player.Character
		local humanoid = character and character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
		if humanoid and character and character:GetAttribute("InLava") == true then
			humanoid:TakeDamage(DAMAGE)
		end
	end
end

function LavaDamage.start(heartbeat: RBXScriptSignal): RBXScriptConnection
	local elapsed = 0
	return heartbeat:Connect(function(dt: number)
		elapsed += dt
		if elapsed < INTERVAL then
			return
		end
		elapsed -= INTERVAL
		LavaDamage.tick()
	end)
end

return LavaDamage
```

- Server script: `LavaDamage.start(game:GetService("RunService").Heartbeat)`. The handler never yields, so exactly one runs per frame and it returns immediately.
- `elapsed -= INTERVAL` (instead of resetting to 0) keeps the average rate at exactly one tick per second even when frames do not divide the interval evenly.
- An equivalent design is `task.spawn(function() while true do task.wait(INTERVAL) LavaDamage.tick() end end)`; both are fine, but do not mix a per-frame event with waits inside it.

Both replicate from server to client and both fire change events. Attributes are properties on the instance itself: no extra objects, cheaper to create, visible in the Properties panel, readable in one call with `GetAttributes`. Value objects are separate instances: they can be referenced, parented, cloned on their own, and ObjectValue can hold an Instance reference, which attributes cannot. Use attributes by default and Value objects when you need an Instance reference or something legacy expects them (leaderstats requires Value objects).

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.DoorState (same logic written both ways)
local DoorState = {}

-- Attribute version: state lives on the door model itself
function DoorState.watchAttribute(door: Instance, onChange: (locked: boolean) -> ()): RBXScriptConnection
	local function emit()
		onChange(door:GetAttribute("Locked") == true)
	end
	emit()
	return door:GetAttributeChangedSignal("Locked"):Connect(emit)
end

-- Value-object version: state lives in a BoolValue child
function DoorState.watchValue(door: Instance, onChange: (locked: boolean) -> ()): RBXScriptConnection?
	local value = door:FindFirstChild("Locked")
	if value == nil or not value:IsA("BoolValue") then
		return nil
	end
	onChange(value.Value)
	return value.Changed:Connect(function()
		onChange(value.Value)
	end)
end

return DoorState
```

- Attribute types are limited to simple data (string, number, boolean, Vector3, CFrame, Color3, UDim2, NumberRange, and similar); tables and Instances are not allowed, and setting an unsupported type errors.
- `ValueBase.Changed` fires only when `Value` changes (and passes the new value), unlike `Changed` on other classes, which fires for every property; `GetAttributeChangedSignal(name)` passes nothing. Reading the current value inside the handler works the same for both.
- Changes made on the client stay on that client in both cases; only server-side changes replicate.

A ModuleScript's code runs once per Luau environment, the first time it is required; the value it returns is cached and every later `require` of the same ModuleScript returns that same value. So two server scripts share one table (and any state stored in it), while the server and each client each run the module separately, with no shared memory between them.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.SessionCounter
-- Everything at the top level runs once per environment (once on the server, once per client).
local createdAt = os.clock()
local counts: { [string]: number } = {}

local SessionCounter = {}

function SessionCounter.bump(key: string): number
	counts[key] = (counts[key] or 0) + 1
	return counts[key]
end

function SessionCounter.get(key: string): number
	return counts[key] or 0
end

function SessionCounter.uptime(): number
	return os.clock() - createdAt
end

return table.freeze(SessionCounter)
```

- Script A calling `SessionCounter.bump("kills")` and Script B calling `SessionCounter.get("kills")` on the server see the same number, because both received the same cached table. A LocalScript requiring it sees its own, separate counts.
- To share data between server and clients, use RemoteEvents, attributes or replicated instances; module state never crosses the network.
- If the module errors while loading, `require` errors too, and later requires of that module fail as well instead of re-running it; fix the error rather than retrying the require.
- `require` yields only if the module's top-level code yields; keep top-level code fast and move waits into functions so requiring the module stays cheap.

answer:
- ServerScriptService: server Scripts and server-only ModuleScripts. Never replicated, so clients cannot read the code.
- ServerStorage: server-only assets (maps, tools to clone); ModuleScripts here also work and are hidden from clients.
- ReplicatedStorage: ModuleScripts and assets both sides need (shared types, config, RemoteEvents).
- ReplicatedFirst: a tiny LocalScript for the loading screen; it runs before anything else replicates.
- StarterPlayerScripts: client code that runs once per session. StarterCharacterScripts: client code copied into each new character, restarting every life.

The common layout is one Script on the server and one LocalScript on the client that require your systems as ModuleScripts and start them in a fixed order, so load order is explicit instead of depending on which Script happens to run first.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Bootstrap (used by the single server Script and the single client LocalScript)
export type System = { name: string?, init: (() -> ())?, start: (() -> ())? }

local Bootstrap = {}

function Bootstrap.run(moduleScripts: { Instance }, load: (ModuleScript) -> any): { string }
	local systems: { { name: string, system: System } } = {}
	for _, moduleScript in moduleScripts do
		if moduleScript:IsA("ModuleScript") then
			table.insert(systems, { name = moduleScript.Name, system = load(moduleScript) :: System })
		end
	end
	table.sort(systems, function(a: { name: string, system: System }, b: { name: string, system: System }): boolean
		return a.name < b.name
	end)
	local started: { string } = {}
	-- phase 1: init everything (create remotes, read config) before any system starts talking to another
	for _, entry in systems do
		if entry.system.init then
			entry.system.init()
		end
	end
	-- phase 2: start (connect events, spawn loops)
	for _, entry in systems do
		if entry.system.start then
			task.spawn(entry.system.start)
		end
		table.insert(started, entry.name)
	end
	return started
end

return Bootstrap
```

- Server Script in ServerScriptService: `Bootstrap.run(ServerScriptService.Systems:GetChildren(), require)`; client LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts does the same with its client systems folder.
- Two phases mean a system's `start` can safely call another system that was set up in `init`, whatever their names.
- `start` runs in `task.spawn`, so a system with a long-running loop does not block the others from starting.

`--!strict` makes the analyzer (Script Editor squiggles, Script Analysis) infer and check types for the whole file and report mismatches such as passing a string where a number is annotated, reading a field that does not exist on a known table type, or using a possibly-nil value without a check. It is purely edit-time: types are erased when the script runs, so nothing is checked at runtime. Data from outside your code (RemoteEvent arguments, DataStore values, JSON, attributes) can still be anything and must be validated by code.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.Gift (static types for callers, runtime checks for the network)
local MAX_GIFT = 1000

local Gift = {}

-- Called by trusted server code: the annotation is enough, the analyzer checks every call site.
function Gift.clampAmount(amount: number): number
	return math.clamp(math.floor(amount), 1, MAX_GIFT)
end

-- Called with values that came from a client: annotate as unknown and check at runtime.
function Gift.parseRequest(targetId: unknown, amount: unknown): (number?, number?)
	if type(targetId) ~= "number" or targetId % 1 ~= 0 or targetId <= 0 then
		return nil, nil
	end
	if type(amount) ~= "number" or amount ~= amount then
		return nil, nil
	end
	return targetId, Gift.clampAmount(amount)
end

return Gift
```

- Strict mode does catch: wrong argument types, missing table fields on typed tables, calling a possibly-nil value, misspelled locals, returning the wrong type. It does not catch: values typed `any` (anything goes, unchecked), wrong values smuggled in with `::` casts, or anything that only happens at runtime.
- `--!nonstrict` (the default) infers less and reports fewer errors; `--!nocheck` turns checking off for the file. The mode never changes how the code executes.
- A function annotated `(amount: number)` will still receive a string at runtime if a remote passes one; that is why network entry points take `unknown` and refine with `type`/`typeof` before calling typed internals.

answer:
- `task.spawn(f)` runs `f` immediately, before the next line of the caller, until `f` yields; then the caller continues.
- `task.defer(f)` queues `f` to run after the current thread (and the rest of the current resumption cycle) finishes, still in the same frame. Use it to let the caller finish its setup first, or to avoid re-entering an event handler while it is still running.
- `task.delay(t, f)` runs `f` after at least `t` seconds, on a later frame. It returns the thread, so `task.cancel` can stop it before it runs.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.SchedulerDemo
local SchedulerDemo = {}

function SchedulerDemo.order(log: { string }): thread
	table.insert(log, "caller start")
	task.spawn(function()
		table.insert(log, "spawn body")
	end)
	task.defer(function()
		table.insert(log, "defer body")
	end)
	local delayed = task.delay(0.5, function()
		table.insert(log, "delay body")
	end)
	table.insert(log, "caller end")
	return delayed
end

-- Typical use of defer: fire "ready" only after the constructor has returned the object to its caller.
function SchedulerDemo.newLoader(onReady: (loader: { ready: boolean }) -> ()): { ready: boolean }
	local loader = { ready = false }
	task.defer(function()
		loader.ready = true
		onReady(loader)
	end)
	return loader
end

return SchedulerDemo
```

- Running `order` logs: caller start, spawn body, caller end, defer body, and then delay body half a second later.
- An error inside a spawned, deferred or delayed function is reported in the output but does not stop the caller, because each runs in its own thread.
- `task.wait(t)` is `task.delay` for the current thread: it yields and resumes after at least `t` seconds; do not use the deprecated globals `spawn`, `delay` and `wait`, which throttle and run late.

`type` only knows the core Luau types (nil, boolean, number, string, table, function, thread, userdata, buffer, vector), so most Roblox values (Instances, CFrames, Color3s) are just "userdata" to it, and Vector3, which is built on Luau's native vector type, reports "vector". `typeof` additionally names Roblox datatypes: "Instance", "Vector3", "CFrame", "Color3", "EnumItem", and so on. Neither tells you the class of an Instance: use `typeof(x) == "Instance"` first, then `x:IsA("BasePart")`, which also accepts subclasses.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Describe
local Describe = {}

function Describe.value(x: unknown): string
	local kind = typeof(x)
	if kind == "Instance" then
		local instance = x :: Instance
		return `Instance<{instance.ClassName}>`
	elseif kind == "EnumItem" then
		return `EnumItem<{tostring(x)}>`
	end
	return kind
end

function Describe.isPart(x: unknown): boolean
	return typeof(x) == "Instance" and (x :: Instance):IsA("BasePart")
end

return Describe
```

- `x.ClassName == "Part"` misses `MeshPart`, `WedgePart` and other subclasses, while `IsA("BasePart")` accepts them all; prefer `IsA` for checks and `ClassName` only for exact display.
- On the server, validate RemoteEvent arguments with `typeof`: `type` would accept a CFrame, a Color3 and an Instance alike as "userdata".
- Calling `x:IsA(...)` on something that is not an Instance errors, which is why the `typeof` check must come first.

answer:
Each easing maps `t` in [0, 1] to an eased alpha with `f(0) = 0` and `f(1) = 1`. A small `progress` helper clamps elapsed/duration so callers never overshoot the end, and `lerp` applies the alpha to numbers.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Easing
export type EasingFn = (t: number) -> number

local Easing = {}

function Easing.linear(t: number): number
	return t
end

function Easing.quadInOut(t: number): number
	return if t < 0.5 then 2 * t * t else 1 - (-2 * t + 2) ^ 2 / 2
end

function Easing.cubicOut(t: number): number
	return 1 - (1 - t) ^ 3
end

function Easing.cubicInOut(t: number): number
	return if t < 0.5 then 4 * t * t * t else 1 - (-2 * t + 2) ^ 3 / 2
end

function Easing.backOut(t: number): number
	local c1 = 1.70158
	local c3 = c1 + 1
	return 1 + c3 * (t - 1) ^ 3 + c1 * (t - 1) ^ 2
end

function Easing.elasticOut(t: number): number
	if t <= 0 or t >= 1 then
		return math.clamp(t, 0, 1)
	end
	return 2 ^ (-10 * t) * math.sin((t * 10 - 0.75) * (2 * math.pi) / 3) + 1
end

function Easing.progress(elapsed: number, duration: number, ease: EasingFn): number
	if duration <= 0 then
		return 1
	end
	return ease(math.clamp(elapsed / duration, 0, 1))
end

function Easing.lerp(a: number, b: number, alpha: number): number
	return a + (b - a) * alpha
end

return Easing
```

- `backOut` and `elasticOut` overshoot past 1 mid-animation by design; that is fine for positions and scale, but clamp before using the alpha for transparency or a progress bar.
- For a moving target, store the start value and start time when the move begins and compute `Easing.lerp(start, target, Easing.progress(now - startTime, 0.4, Easing.cubicOut))` each frame; for CFrames use `start:Lerp(goal, alpha)`.
- `progress` with a zero duration returns 1, so an instant transition snaps to the end instead of dividing by zero.

Put the types in one ModuleScript with `export type`, and give it a constructor that is the only place quest tables are built. Other scripts `require` it and refer to `QuestTypes.Quest`.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Shared.QuestTypes
export type QuestStatus = "Locked" | "Active" | "Completed"

export type Objective = {
	description: string,
	required: number,
	progress: number,
}

export type Quest = {
	id: string,
	title: string,
	status: QuestStatus,
	objectives: { Objective },
	rewardCoins: number,
}

local QuestTypes = {}

function QuestTypes.newQuest(id: string, title: string, rewardCoins: number, goals: { [string]: number }): Quest
	local objectives: { Objective } = {}
	for description, required in goals do
		table.insert(objectives, { description = description, required = math.max(1, required), progress = 0 })
	end
	table.sort(objectives, function(a: Objective, b: Objective): boolean
		return a.description < b.description
	end)
	return { id = id, title = title, status = "Locked", objectives = objectives, rewardCoins = rewardCoins }
end

function QuestTypes.isComplete(quest: Quest): boolean
	for _, objective in quest.objectives do
		if objective.progress < objective.required then
			return false
		end
	end
	return true
end

return QuestTypes
```

- In a consumer: `local QuestTypes = require(ReplicatedStorage.Shared.QuestTypes)`, then `type Quest = QuestTypes.Quest` and `local function addProgress(quest: Quest, amount: number)`. The alias is local; the source of truth stays in one file.
- The require path must be a static expression (`ReplicatedStorage.Shared.QuestTypes`, not a string built at runtime) or the analyzer cannot see the exported types.
- `QuestStatus` is a union of string literals, so `quest.status = "Done"` is rejected by the analyzer.
- Types are erased at runtime: exporting them costs nothing and does not add fields to the module table.

Use an accumulator: add each frame's `dt`, run the simulation in fixed steps while enough time is banked, and keep the remainder for next frame. Cap the steps per frame so a long hitch cannot cause a spiral of catch-up work, and expose the leftover fraction for render interpolation.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.FixedStep
export type FixedStep = {
	step: number,
	maxSteps: number,
	accumulator: number,
	ticks: number,
}

local FixedStep = {}

function FixedStep.new(hz: number, maxSteps: number?): FixedStep
	assert(hz > 0, "rate must be positive")
	return { step = 1 / hz, maxSteps = maxSteps or 5, accumulator = 0, ticks = 0 }
end

-- Returns the interpolation alpha in [0, 1) between the last two simulated states.
function FixedStep.advance(self: FixedStep, dt: number, simulate: (step: number, tick: number) -> ()): number
	self.accumulator += math.max(dt, 0)
	local steps = 0
	while self.accumulator >= self.step and steps < self.maxSteps do
		self.accumulator -= self.step
		self.ticks += 1
		steps += 1
		simulate(self.step, self.ticks)
	end
	if steps == self.maxSteps and self.accumulator >= self.step then
		-- too far behind: drop the backlog instead of trying to catch up forever
		self.accumulator %= self.step
	end
	return self.accumulator / self.step
end

return FixedStep
```

```lua
--!strict
-- LocalScript usage: a ball simulated at 60 Hz, rendered every frame
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local FixedStep = require(ReplicatedStorage.FixedStep)

local ball = workspace:WaitForChild("Ball") :: BasePart
local clock = FixedStep.new(60)
local gravity = Vector3.new(0, -workspace.Gravity, 0)
local position, velocity = ball.Position, Vector3.new(20, 40, 0)
local previous = position

		previous = position
		velocity += gravity * step

	end)

end)
```

- Every machine runs exactly the same sequence of 1/60 s steps, so the trajectory matches across frame rates.
- `maxSteps` bounds the work per frame; after a long freeze the simulation slows down briefly instead of locking up while running hundreds of steps.

Work in whole seconds (floor once at the top, clamp negatives to zero), split into units with `//` and `%`, and format each style from those parts. Do not use `os.date` for durations: it formats calendar times and is affected by the time zone.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Duration
local Duration = {}

local function parts(seconds: number): (number, number, number, number)
	local s = math.max(0, math.floor(seconds))
	return s // 86400, s % 86400 // 3600, s % 3600 // 60, s % 60
end

function Duration.clock(seconds: number): string
	local days, hours, minutes, secs = parts(seconds)
	hours += days * 24
	if hours > 0 then
		return string.format("%d:%02d:%02d", hours, minutes, secs)
	end
	return string.format("%d:%02d", minutes, secs)
end

function Duration.compact(seconds: number, maxUnits: number?): string
	local days, hours, minutes, secs = parts(seconds)
	local limit = maxUnits or 2
	local out: { string } = {}
	for _, unit in { { days, "d" }, { hours, "h" }, { minutes, "m" }, { secs, "s" } } do
		local amount, label = unit[1] :: number, unit[2] :: string
		if amount > 0 and #out < limit then
			table.insert(out, `{amount}{label}`)
		end
	end
	return if #out == 0 then "0s" else table.concat(out, " ")
end

function Duration.ago(seconds: number): string
	local s = math.max(0, math.floor(seconds))
	local function plural(n: number, word: string): string
		return `{n} {word}{if n == 1 then "" else "s"} ago`
	end
	if s < 60 then
		return "just now"
	elseif s < 3600 then
		return plural(s // 60, "minute")
	elseif s < 86400 then
		return plural(s // 3600, "hour")
	end
	return plural(s // 86400, "day")
end

return Duration
```

- Floor once at the top: a countdown at 59.9 s shows `0:59`, never `0:60` from rounding each part separately.
- `compact` skips zero units and stops at `maxUnits`, so 1 day 0 hours 5 minutes shows as "1d 5m" with the default of two units.
- For a countdown to an event, compute `endUnix - workspace:GetServerTimeNow()` so every client agrees regardless of its local clock.

Type the config shape, then deep-freeze it before returning. `table.freeze` is shallow, so nested tables need freezing too; any later write raises an error at the line that tried it.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Config
export type WeaponStats = {
	Damage: number,
	FireRate: number,
	MagazineSize: number,
}

export type Config = {
	MaxPlayers: number,
	RoundSeconds: number,
	Weapons: { [string]: WeaponStats },
}

local function deepFreeze<T>(value: T): T
	if type(value) == "table" and not table.isfrozen(value) then
		for _, child in value :: any do
			deepFreeze(child)
		end
		table.freeze(value :: any)
	end
	return value
end

local config: Config = {
	MaxPlayers = 12,
	RoundSeconds = 180,
	Weapons = {
		Rifle = { Damage = 22, FireRate = 8, MagazineSize = 30 },
		Shotgun = { Damage = 9, FireRate = 1.2, MagazineSize = 6 },
	},
}

return deepFreeze(config)
```

- A write to a frozen table errors with "attempt to modify a readonly table", so the stray test edit fails loudly instead of leaking into other scripts.
- Code that needs a tweaked copy (a power-up, a test) should use `table.clone(Config.Weapons.Rifle)`; the clone is not frozen.
- Freezing happens once at require time, and reads from a frozen table cost the same as reads from a normal one.

answer:
A pool that keeps a stack of released objects, hands them out before creating new ones, and runs a reset callback on release so stale state never leaks into the next user. A cap on the free list stops a burst from pinning memory forever.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Pool
export type Pool<T> = {
	acquire: (self: Pool<T>) -> T,
	release: (self: Pool<T>, object: T) -> (),
	stats: (self: Pool<T>) -> (number, number),
}

local Pool = {}

function Pool.new<T>(create: () -> T, reset: (T) -> (), maxFree: number?): Pool<T>
	local free: { T } = {}
	local inUse: { [T]: boolean } = {}
	local cap = maxFree or 256
	local pool = {} :: Pool<T>

	function pool.acquire(_self: Pool<T>): T
		local object = free[#free]
		if object ~= nil then
			free[#free] = nil
		else
			object = create()
		end
		inUse[object] = true
		return object
	end

	function pool.release(_self: Pool<T>, object: T): ()
		if not inUse[object] then
			error("released an object this pool did not hand out (or released it twice)", 2)
		end
		inUse[object] = nil
		reset(object)
		if #free < cap then
			table.insert(free, object)
		end
	end

	function pool.stats(_self: Pool<T>): (number, number)
		local active = 0
		for _ in inUse do
			active += 1
		end
		return active, #free
	end

	return pool
end

return Pool
```

- Usage: `local sparks = Pool.new(function() return { pos = Vector3.zero, vel = Vector3.zero, life = 0 } end, function(s) s.life = 0 end)`.
- Double release is the classic pool bug (two systems end up sharing one object); the `inUse` set turns it into an immediate error at the faulty call.
- Pools pay off for objects created at high rates; for a few allocations per second the GC handles it fine and the extra bookkeeping is not worth it.

answer:
A generic `Queue<T>` that keeps head and tail indices, so push and pop are O(1) with no shifting. The type parameter flows from `Queue.new()` into every method.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Queue
export type Queue<T> = {
	push: (self: Queue<T>, value: T) -> (),
	pop: (self: Queue<T>) -> T?,
	peek: (self: Queue<T>) -> T?,
	size: (self: Queue<T>) -> number,
	_items: { [number]: T },
	_head: number,
	_tail: number,
}

local Queue = {}

local function push<T>(self: Queue<T>, value: T): ()
	self._tail += 1
	self._items[self._tail] = value
end

local function pop<T>(self: Queue<T>): T?
	if self._head > self._tail then
		return nil
	end
	local value = self._items[self._head]
	self._items[self._head] = nil
	self._head += 1
	if self._head > self._tail then
		-- empty again: reset so the indices never grow without bound
		self._head, self._tail = 1, 0
	end
	return value
end

local function peek<T>(self: Queue<T>): T?
	return self._items[self._head]
end

local function size<T>(self: Queue<T>): number
	return self._tail - self._head + 1
end

function Queue.new<T>(): Queue<T>
	return {
		push = push,
		pop = pop,
		peek = peek,
		size = size,
		_items = {},
		_head = 1,
		_tail = 0,
	}
end

return Queue
```

- Usage: `local spawns: Queue.Queue<Player> = Queue.new()`; then `spawns:push(player)` rejects anything that is not a Player.
- `pop` returns `T?`, so strict mode forces callers to handle the empty case: `local nextPlayer = spawns:pop(); if nextPlayer then ... end`.
- Popped slots are set to nil so the queue does not keep references to removed players alive.

`a // b` is floor division (same as `math.floor(a / b)`, including for negatives) and `x += 1` style compound assignment evaluates the target once. Both fit index math well.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.TileGrid
export type TileGrid = {
	width: number,
	height: number,
	tileSize: number,
	origin: Vector3,
	tiles: { number },
}

local TileGrid = {}

function TileGrid.new(width: number, height: number, tileSize: number, origin: Vector3): TileGrid
	return { width = width, height = height, tileSize = tileSize, origin = origin, tiles = table.create(width * height, 0) }
end

function TileGrid.toIndex(grid: TileGrid, x: number, y: number): number?
	if x < 0 or y < 0 or x >= grid.width or y >= grid.height then
		return nil
	end
	return y * grid.width + x + 1
end

function TileGrid.fromIndex(grid: TileGrid, index: number): (number, number)
	local zeroBased = index - 1
	return zeroBased % grid.width, zeroBased // grid.width
end

function TileGrid.worldToTile(grid: TileGrid, position: Vector3): (number, number)
	local offset = position - grid.origin
	return offset.X // grid.tileSize, offset.Z // grid.tileSize
end

function TileGrid.addGrowth(grid: TileGrid, x: number, y: number, amount: number): boolean
	local index = TileGrid.toIndex(grid, x, y)
	if index == nil then
		return false
	end
	grid.tiles[index] += amount
	grid.tiles[index] = math.min(grid.tiles[index], 100)
	return true
end

return TileGrid
```

- `//` floors toward negative infinity, so a position 0.5 studs left of the origin maps to tile `-1`, not `0`; `toIndex` then rejects it instead of wrapping onto the wrong row.
- `grid.tiles[index] += amount` indexes `grid.tiles` once; with longer expressions such as `self.cache[key()] += 1` that avoids calling `key()` twice.
- `table.create(n, 0)` preallocates the array, which matters for big plots that are filled right away.

`a and b or c` returns `c` whenever `b` is falsy, so it breaks exactly when the "true" value is `nil` or `false`. Luau's `if cond then x else y` expression evaluates only the chosen branch and returns `x` even when it is falsy.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Badge
local Badge = {}

function Badge.badgeFor(rank: number, isVip: boolean): (string, Color3?, boolean)
	local color: Color3? = if isVip then nil else Color3.new(1, 1, 1)
	local label = if rank >= 100 then "Legend"
		elseif rank >= 50 then "Veteran"
		elseif rank >= 10 then "Regular"
		else "Newbie"
	local showCrown = not isVip
	return label, color, showCrown
end

return Badge
```

- In the original, `isVip and nil or white` is white for VIPs too, and `isVip and false or true` is always `true`; both had the falsy-middle problem.

answer:
Luau's generalized iteration calls the `__iter` metamethod if the value has one, otherwise it iterates the table like `pairs` (array part in order first). Give the class an `__iter` that returns a stateless iterator over a sorted snapshot.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Leaderboard
export type Entry = { name: string, score: number }

local Leaderboard = {}
Leaderboard.__index = Leaderboard

type Fields = { _scores: { [string]: number } }
export type Leaderboard = typeof(setmetatable({} :: Fields, Leaderboard))

function Leaderboard.new(): Leaderboard
	return setmetatable({ _scores = {} } :: Fields, Leaderboard)
end

function Leaderboard.add(self: Leaderboard, name: string, points: number): ()
	self._scores[name] = (self._scores[name] or 0) + points
end

function Leaderboard.sorted(self: Leaderboard): { Entry }
	local list: { Entry } = {}
	for name, score in self._scores do
		table.insert(list, { name = name, score = score })
	end
	table.sort(list, function(a: Entry, b: Entry): boolean
		if a.score ~= b.score then
			return a.score > b.score
		end
		return a.name < b.name
	end)
	return list
end

function Leaderboard.__iter(self: Leaderboard)
	local list = Leaderboard.sorted(self)
	local function step(entries: { Entry }, rank: number): (number?, Entry?)
		local nextRank = rank + 1
		local entry = entries[nextRank]
		if entry == nil then
			return nil, nil
		end
		return nextRank, entry
	end
	return step, list, 0
end

return Leaderboard
```

- `for rank, entry in board do` now yields `1, {name, score}`, `2, ...` in score order; ties break by name so the order is stable between refreshes.
- Plain tables need no `pairs`/`ipairs`: `for i, v in list do` walks the array part in order, then the hash part.
- `__iter` builds a snapshot, so adding scores during the loop does not disturb the iteration.

Make the state a union of string literals; assignments of any other string fail to type-check. For exhaustiveness, end the `if` chain with a branch that assigns the remaining value to `never`: once every state is handled the branch type-checks, and a forgotten state turns it into an error.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.DoorLogic
export type DoorState = "Closed" | "Opening" | "Open" | "Locked"
export type DoorInput = "Use" | "Unlock" | "Lock" | "Finished"

local DoorLogic = {}

function DoorLogic.next(state: DoorState, input: DoorInput, hasKey: boolean): DoorState
	if state == "Closed" then
		if input == "Use" then
			return "Opening"
		elseif input == "Lock" and hasKey then
			return "Locked"
		end
		return "Closed"
	elseif state == "Opening" then
		return if input == "Finished" then "Open" else "Opening"
	elseif state == "Open" then
		return if input == "Use" then "Closed" else "Open"
	elseif state == "Locked" then
		return if input == "Unlock" and hasKey then "Closed" else "Locked"
	else
		local unhandled: never = state
		error(`unhandled door state {unhandled}`)
	end
end

function DoorLogic.isPassable(state: DoorState): boolean
	return state == "Open"
end

return DoorLogic
```

- `DoorLogic.next("Opened", "Use", false)` is rejected: `"Opened"` is not part of `DoorState`.

answer:
Combine a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. `get` moves the node to the front, `set` inserts at the front and evicts from the back when over capacity; every operation touches a constant number of nodes.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.LruCache
type Node<K, V> = { key: K, value: V, prev: Node<K, V>?, next: Node<K, V>? }

export type LruCache<K, V> = {
	capacity: number,
	size: number,
	map: { [K]: Node<K, V> },
	head: Node<K, V>?, -- most recently used
	tail: Node<K, V>?, -- least recently used
}

local LruCache = {}

function LruCache.new<K, V>(capacity: number): LruCache<K, V>
	assert(capacity >= 1, "capacity must be at least 1")
	return { capacity = capacity, size = 0, map = {}, head = nil, tail = nil }
end

local function unlink<K, V>(cache: LruCache<K, V>, node: Node<K, V>)
	if node.prev then
		node.prev.next = node.next
	else
		cache.head = node.next
	end
	if node.next then
		node.next.prev = node.prev
	else
		cache.tail = node.prev
	end
	node.prev, node.next = nil, nil
end

local function pushFront<K, V>(cache: LruCache<K, V>, node: Node<K, V>)
	node.next = cache.head
	if cache.head then
		cache.head.prev = node
	end
	cache.head = node
	if cache.tail == nil then
		cache.tail = node
	end
end

function LruCache.get<K, V>(cache: LruCache<K, V>, key: K): V?
	local node = cache.map[key]
	if node == nil then
		return nil
	end
	unlink(cache, node)
	pushFront(cache, node)
	return node.value
end

function LruCache.set<K, V>(cache: LruCache<K, V>, key: K, value: V): ()
	local node = cache.map[key]
	if node then
		node.value = value
		unlink(cache, node)
		pushFront(cache, node)
		return
	end
	local fresh: Node<K, V> = { key = key, value = value, prev = nil, next = nil }
	cache.map[key] = fresh
	pushFront(cache, fresh)
	cache.size += 1
	if cache.size > cache.capacity then
		local oldest = cache.tail
		if oldest then
			unlink(cache, oldest)
			cache.map[oldest.key] = nil
			cache.size -= 1
		end
	end
end

return LruCache
```

- Usage: `local summaries: LruCache.LruCache<number, Summary> = LruCache.new(500)`; on a miss, fetch, then `LruCache.set(summaries, userId, result)`.
- A cache hit refreshes recency, so popular entries stay while one-off lookups age out at the tail.
- Cache only successful fetches; storing an error result would serve the failure until it is evicted. Add a timestamp to the value if entries should also expire by age.

answer:
Pick the suffix from the exponent, round to the wanted decimals, and if rounding pushed the value to 1000 move up one suffix (the "1000K" bug). Trailing zeros are stripped so 2.50K shows as 2.5K. The comma formatter works on the integer digits as a string.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.NumberFormat
local SUFFIXES = { "", "K", "M", "B", "T", "Qa", "Qi", "Sx", "Sp", "Oc", "No", "Dc" }

local NumberFormat = {}

local function trimZeros(s: string): string
	if string.find(s, "%.") then
		s = string.gsub(s, "0+$", "")
		s = string.gsub(s, "%.$", "")
	end
	return s
end

function NumberFormat.abbreviate(value: number, decimals: number?): string
	if value ~= value then
		return "0"
	end
	local places = decimals or 2
	local sign = if value < 0 then "-" else ""
	local n = math.abs(value)
	if n < 1000 then
		return sign .. trimZeros(string.format(`%.{places}f`, math.floor(n * 10 ^ places) / 10 ^ places))
	end
	local tier = math.min(math.floor(math.log10(n) / 3), #SUFFIXES - 1)
	local scaled = n / 10 ^ (tier * 3)
	local factor = 10 ^ places
	scaled = math.floor(scaled * factor + 0.5) / factor
	if scaled >= 1000 and tier < #SUFFIXES - 1 then
		tier += 1
		scaled /= 1000
	end
	return sign .. trimZeros(string.format(`%.{places}f`, scaled)) .. SUFFIXES[tier + 1]
end

function NumberFormat.commas(value: number): string
	local sign = if value < 0 then "-" else ""
	local digits = string.format("%d", math.floor(math.abs(value)))
	local formatted = string.reverse((string.gsub(string.reverse(digits), "(%d%d%d)", "%1,")))
	if string.sub(formatted, 1, 1) == "," then
		formatted = string.sub(formatted, 2)
	end
	return sign .. formatted
end

return NumberFormat
```

- `999999` rounds to `1000.00K`, which the post-rounding check turns into `1M`.
- Values below 1000 are floored, not rounded, so a player with 9.999 coins never sees "10" and then fails to buy a 10-coin item.
- Numbers above about 2^53 lose integer precision in Luau, so `commas` on huge values shows rounded digits; switch big economies to the abbreviated form only.

answer:
Narrow optionals once at the boundary: a small helper returns `BasePart?`, callers early-`continue` or early-return on nil, and after that check the analyzer treats the value as non-nil. The final result is itself optional so the caller must handle "nobody in range".

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.Targeting
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local Targeting = {}

local function rootOf(player: Player): BasePart?
	local character = player.Character
	if character == nil then
		return nil
	end
	local humanoid = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
	if humanoid == nil or humanoid.Health <= 0 then
		return nil
	end
	local root = character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart")
	if root and root:IsA("BasePart") then
		return root
	end
	return nil
end

function Targeting.nearestPlayer(origin: Vector3, maxRange: number): (Player?, number)
	local best: Player? = nil
	local bestDistance = maxRange
	for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
		local root = rootOf(player)
		if root == nil then
			continue
		end
		local distance = (root.Position - origin).Magnitude
		if distance <= bestDistance then
			best, bestDistance = player, distance
		end
	end
	return best, bestDistance
end

return Targeting
```

- `root and root:IsA("BasePart")` both removes nil and refines the Instance to a BasePart, so `.Position` needs no cast.
- Casting with `::` only silences the analyzer and does nothing at runtime; when the character is mid-respawn the next `.Position` read still errors. Refinement handles that case.
- Caller pattern: `local target = Targeting.nearestPlayer(npcPos, 60); if target then ... end`. Dead players are skipped so NPCs do not chase a corpse.

answer:
Mark changes in a per-player "dirty" table as they happen (cheap, no network), and flush on a fixed interval: one remote call per player carrying only the keys that changed, with the latest value for each. Many changes to the same key collapse into one entry.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.UpdateBatcher
export type Batcher = {
	set: (self: Batcher, player: Player, key: string, value: number) -> (),
	flush: (self: Batcher) -> number,
	forget: (self: Batcher, player: Player) -> (),
}

local UpdateBatcher = {}

function UpdateBatcher.new(remote: RemoteEvent): Batcher
	local dirty: { [Player]: { [string]: number } } = {}
	local batcher = {} :: Batcher

	function batcher.set(_self: Batcher, player: Player, key: string, value: number)
		local changes = dirty[player]
		if changes == nil then
			changes = {}
			dirty[player] = changes
		end
		changes[key] = value -- later values overwrite earlier ones; only the latest is sent
	end

	function batcher.flush(_self: Batcher): number
		local sent = 0
		local pending = dirty
		dirty = {}
		for player, changes in pending do
			if player.Parent ~= nil then
				remote:FireClient(player, changes)
				sent += 1
			end
		end
		return sent
	end

	function batcher.forget(_self: Batcher, player: Player)
		dirty[player] = nil
	end

	return batcher
end

function UpdateBatcher.autoFlush(batcher: Batcher, heartbeat: RBXScriptSignal, interval: number): RBXScriptConnection
	local elapsed = 0
	return heartbeat:Connect(function(dt: number)
		elapsed += dt
		if elapsed >= interval then
			elapsed = 0
			batcher:flush()
		end
	end)
end

return UpdateBatcher
```

- Server wiring: `local batcher = UpdateBatcher.new(statsRemote)`, `UpdateBatcher.autoFlush(batcher, RunService.Heartbeat, 0.2)`, `Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(p) batcher:forget(p) end)`, and droppers call `batcher:set(player, "Ore", newTotal)`.
- Sending absolute values (the new total) rather than deltas means a dropped or merged update can never desynchronise the client.
- Five updates per second is plenty for UI; the client can tween the displayed number toward the latest value to hide the step.

answer:
Collect the parts and their target CFrames into two arrays and move them with one `BulkMoveTo` call per frame. Pass `Enum.BulkMoveMode.FireCFrameChanged` so only CFrame change events fire, which is cheaper than the default of firing every property event. Reuse the two arrays every frame so the batch itself does not allocate.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.ConveyorMover
export type Item = { part: BasePart, distance: number }
export type Path = { origin: CFrame, direction: Vector3, length: number }

local ConveyorMover = {}

local partsBuffer: { BasePart } = {}
local cframesBuffer: { CFrame } = {}

function ConveyorMover.step(items: { Item }, path: Path, speed: number, dt: number): number
	table.clear(partsBuffer)
	table.clear(cframesBuffer)
	local wrapped = 0
	for _, entry in items do
		entry.distance += speed * dt
		if entry.distance > path.length then
			entry.distance -= path.length
			wrapped += 1
		end
		table.insert(partsBuffer, entry.part)
		table.insert(cframesBuffer, path.origin + path.direction * entry.distance)
	end
	workspace:BulkMoveTo(partsBuffer, cframesBuffer, Enum.BulkMoveMode.FireCFrameChanged)
	return wrapped
end

return ConveyorMover
```

- `BulkMoveTo` skips the per-assignment property overhead and updates the parts as one batch; it works best for anchored parts you move every frame.
- With `FireCFrameChanged`, listeners on `Position` or `Orientation` stop firing; if some script relies on those, pass `Enum.BulkMoveMode.FireAllEvents` (the default) instead.
- Purely visual movement like this can also run on each client instead of the server, which removes the replication cost of 400 moving parts entirely.

answer:
Each lookup is cheap alone, but inside players x zones x 60 frames they add up and also allocate (`GetChildren` returns a new table every call). Resolve things once: services at the top, the zone list once (updated by events), and each player's root part when the character spawns, then the hot loop only reads cached references.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.ZoneWatch
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

export type Zone = { name: string, center: Vector3, radiusSq: number }

local ZoneWatch = {}

local roots: { [Player]: BasePart } = {}
local zones: { Zone } = {}

local function track(player: Player)
	local function onCharacter(character: Model)
		roots[player] = nil
		local root = character:WaitForChild("HumanoidRootPart", 10)
		if root and root:IsA("BasePart") and player.Character == character then
			roots[player] = root
		end
	end
	player.CharacterAdded:Connect(onCharacter)
	player.CharacterRemoving:Connect(function()
		roots[player] = nil
	end)
	if player.Character then
		task.spawn(onCharacter, player.Character)
	end
end

function ZoneWatch.start(zoneFolder: Instance): ()
	local function rebuild()
		table.clear(zones)
		for _, part in zoneFolder:GetChildren() do
			if part:IsA("BasePart") then
				local r = part.Size.X / 2
				table.insert(zones, { name = part.Name, center = part.Position, radiusSq = r * r })
			end
		end
	end
	rebuild()
	zoneFolder.ChildAdded:Connect(rebuild)
	zoneFolder.ChildRemoved:Connect(rebuild)
	Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(track)
	Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player: Player)
		roots[player] = nil
	end)
	for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
		track(player)
	end
end

-- Hot path: called every frame; only cached reads and arithmetic.
function ZoneWatch.occupancy(out: { [string]: number }): { [string]: number }
	table.clear(out)
	for _, root in roots do
		local p = root.Position
		for _, zone in zones do
			local d = p - zone.center
			if d.X * d.X + d.Z * d.Z <= zone.radiusSq then
				out[zone.name] = (out[zone.name] or 0) + 1
			end
		end
	end
	return out
end

return ZoneWatch
```

- `roots` drops entries on `CharacterRemoving` and `PlayerRemoving`, so cached references never point at destroyed parts and the table does not leak.
- Zones are static in most maps; rebuilding the cached list on `ChildAdded`/`ChildRemoved` keeps it correct if you add zones at runtime without paying for `GetChildren` each frame.
- `occupancy` fills a caller-owned table, so the per-frame call allocates nothing. Profile first: if this loop is under 0.1 ms, readability wins over further tuning.

answer:
Decorative meshes that nothing collides with should not be collidable, queryable or touchable, and need only the cheapest collision geometry: `CanCollide`, `CanQuery` and `CanTouch` false and `CollisionFidelity` `Box`. Background props that players never inspect up close can use `RenderFidelity` `Performance`. `CollisionFidelity` and `RenderFidelity` cannot be changed by game scripts at runtime, so run this once from the Studio command bar (or a plugin) on the folder of props, then save the place.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerStorage.Tools.PropOptimizer (run from the command bar in Studio:
--   require(game:GetService("ServerStorage").Tools.PropOptimizer).apply(workspace.Props, false))
export type Report = { scanned: number, changed: number, skippedCollidable: number }

local PropOptimizer = {}

function PropOptimizer.apply(root: Instance, dryRun: boolean): Report
	local report: Report = { scanned = 0, changed = 0, skippedCollidable = 0 }
	for _, part in root:GetDescendants() do
		if not part:IsA("MeshPart") then
			continue
		end
		report.scanned += 1
		if part:GetAttribute("KeepCollision") == true then
			report.skippedCollidable += 1
			continue -- props players stand on or that block bullets keep their settings
		end
		local needsChange = part.CanCollide or part.CanQuery or part.CanTouch
			or part.CollisionFidelity ~= Enum.CollisionFidelity.Box
			or part.RenderFidelity ~= Enum.RenderFidelity.Performance
		if needsChange then
			report.changed += 1
			if not dryRun then
				part.CanCollide = false
				part.CanQuery = false
				part.CanTouch = false
				part.CollisionFidelity = Enum.CollisionFidelity.Box
				part.RenderFidelity = Enum.RenderFidelity.Performance
			end
		end
	end
	return report
end

return PropOptimizer
```

- Run with `dryRun = true` first to see how many parts would change; mark exceptions (a rock players climb) with a `KeepCollision` attribute.
- `CanQuery = false` also removes the part from raycasts and spatial queries, which speeds up every gun and placement check in the game; leave it on for anything bullets should hit.
- `RenderFidelity.Performance` always renders the lowest-detail version of the mesh; keep `Automatic` (detail drops only with distance) on hero props players see up close, which you can also mark with the attribute.
- Anchor static props as well: unanchored decoration costs physics simulation even when it never moves.

answer:
Wrap each system's update in `debug.profilebegin(label)` / `debug.profileend()`; the label then appears as its own bar inside Heartbeat. A small runner calls each system in `pcall` so `profileend` always runs, and also keeps a rolling average per system that you can print without opening the profiler.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.SystemRunner
export type System = { name: string, update: (dt: number) -> () }
export type Runner = { systems: { System }, avgMs: { [string]: number }, errors: { [string]: number } }

local SMOOTHING = 0.05

local SystemRunner = {}

function SystemRunner.new(systems: { System }): Runner
	return { systems = systems, avgMs = {}, errors = {} }
end

function SystemRunner.step(runner: Runner, dt: number): ()
	for _, system in runner.systems do
		local started = os.clock()
		debug.profilebegin(system.name)
		local ok, err = pcall(system.update, dt)
		debug.profileend() -- always paired with profilebegin, even when update errored
		local ms = (os.clock() - started) * 1000
		local previous = runner.avgMs[system.name]
		runner.avgMs[system.name] = if previous then previous + (ms - previous) * SMOOTHING else ms
		if not ok then
			runner.errors[system.name] = (runner.errors[system.name] or 0) + 1
			warn(`[{system.name}] {err}`)
		end
	end
end

function SystemRunner.report(runner: Runner): string
	local lines: { string } = {}
	for _, system in runner.systems do
		local avg = runner.avgMs[system.name] or 0
		table.insert(lines, string.format("%-12s %6.3f ms  errors %d", system.name, avg, runner.errors[system.name] or 0))
	end
	return table.concat(lines, "\n")
end

return SystemRunner
```

- Wiring: `local runner = SystemRunner.new({ { name = "AI", update = AI.update }, { name = "Loot", update = Loot.update } })` and `RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function(dt) SystemRunner.step(runner, dt) end)`; each name then appears nested under Heartbeat. Ctrl+F6 opens the client MicroProfiler; for this server loop, record from the MicroProfiler tab of the Developer Console in server mode.
- An unpaired `profilebegin` corrupts the profiler's nesting for the rest of the frame, which is why the update runs in `pcall` and `profileend` comes right after it.
- Labels should be constant strings; building them per call (`"AI " .. npc.Name`) allocates every frame and floods the profiler with unique bars.

answer:
Split the work into a pure function (noise math, no Instance writes) that runs in the parallel phase, and a short serial phase that writes the results to the world. Several Actors each receive chunk requests by message; inside the handler the math runs desynchronized, then `task.synchronize()` switches back before touching Terrain.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.ChunkMath (pure: safe to call in parallel)
local ChunkMath = {}

export type Params = { size: number, scale: number, amplitude: number, seed: number }

function ChunkMath.heights(chunkX: number, chunkZ: number, p: Params): { number }
	local out = table.create(p.size * p.size, 0)
	local i = 0
	for z = 0, p.size - 1 do
		for x = 0, p.size - 1 do
			i += 1
			local wx = (chunkX * p.size + x) * p.scale
			local wz = (chunkZ * p.size + z) * p.scale
			-- two octaves of noise; math.noise is deterministic for the same inputs
			local n = math.noise(wx, wz, p.seed) + 0.5 * math.noise(wx * 2, wz * 2, p.seed + 17)
			out[i] = math.floor((n + 1.5) / 3 * p.amplitude)
		end
	end
	return out
end

return ChunkMath
```

```lua
--!strict
-- Script inside each Actor (ServerScriptService.ChunkWorkers.Worker1.Worker, ...)
local ServerScriptService = game:GetService("ServerScriptService")
local ChunkMath = require(ServerScriptService.ChunkMath)

local PARAMS = { size = 64, scale = 0.02, amplitude = 40, seed = 12345 }
local CELL = 4

local actor = script:GetActor()
actor:BindToMessageParallel("Generate", function(chunkX: number, chunkZ: number)
	-- parallel phase: pure math only, no writes to the DataModel
	local heights = ChunkMath.heights(chunkX, chunkZ, PARAMS)

	task.synchronize() -- serial phase: now it is safe to modify Terrain
	local i = 0
	for z = 0, PARAMS.size - 1 do
		for x = 0, PARAMS.size - 1 do
			i += 1
			local h = math.max(1, heights[i])
			local position = Vector3.new((chunkX * PARAMS.size + x) * CELL, h / 2, (chunkZ * PARAMS.size + z) * CELL)
			workspace.Terrain:FillBlock(CFrame.new(position), Vector3.new(CELL, h, CELL), Enum.Material.Grass)
		end
	end
end)
```

```lua
--!strict
-- Script: ServerScriptService.ChunkDispatcher (sends requests round-robin to the Actors)
local ServerScriptService = game:GetService("ServerScriptService")
local workers = ServerScriptService:WaitForChild("ChunkWorkers"):GetChildren()

local nextWorker = 1
local function requestChunk(chunkX: number, chunkZ: number)
	local actor = workers[nextWorker] :: Actor
	nextWorker = nextWorker % #workers + 1
	actor:SendMessage("Generate", chunkX, chunkZ)
end

for cx = -2, 2 do
	for cz = -2, 2 do
		requestChunk(cx, cz)
	end
end
```

- Work only spreads across cores when it is split over several Actors; code inside one Actor runs on one thread. Four to eight workers is a reasonable start.
- In the parallel phase you may read Instances and call pure functions, but property writes, `Instance.new` parenting and most engine mutations error until `task.synchronize()`. Use `task.desynchronize()` to enter the parallel phase from serial code that is not already running in a parallel handler.
- Keep the serial part short: if writing to Terrain dominates, batch it with `Terrain:WriteVoxels` over a region instead of one `FillBlock` per cell.

answer:
Yes: creating and parenting a part is far more expensive than moving one. Pre-create parts once, keep them parented, and "hide" free ones by moving them far away instead of changing `Parent` (which triggers replication/hierarchy work). A tracer then only sets `CFrame`, `Size` and `Transparency`.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.TracerPool (client)
local PARK = CFrame.new(0, 10e6, 0)

export type TracerPool = {
	free: { BasePart },
	inUse: { [BasePart]: boolean },
	folder: Instance,
	template: BasePart,
}

local TracerPool = {}

local function makePart(pool: TracerPool): BasePart
	local part = pool.template:Clone()
	part.Anchored = true
	part.CanCollide = false
	part.CanQuery = false
	part.CanTouch = false
	part.CFrame = PARK
	part.Parent = pool.folder
	return part
end

function TracerPool.new(template: BasePart, folder: Instance, prewarm: number): TracerPool
	local pool: TracerPool = { free = {}, inUse = {}, folder = folder, template = template }
	for _ = 1, prewarm do
		table.insert(pool.free, makePart(pool))
	end
	return pool
end

function TracerPool.show(pool: TracerPool, from: Vector3, to: Vector3, lifetime: number): BasePart
	local part = table.remove(pool.free) or makePart(pool)
	pool.inUse[part] = true
	local length = (to - from).Magnitude
	part.Size = Vector3.new(0.1, 0.1, length)
	part.CFrame = CFrame.lookAt((from + to) / 2, to)
	part.Transparency = 0.2
	task.delay(lifetime, function()
		if pool.inUse[part] then
			pool.inUse[part] = nil
			part.CFrame = PARK
			table.insert(pool.free, part)
		end
	end)
	return part
end

return TracerPool
```

- Prewarm to your typical peak (for example 60) during loading so the first burst does not create parts mid-fight; the pool still grows if a burst exceeds it.
- Parking far away keeps the parts parented, so reuse is a property change instead of a hierarchy change; `CanQuery`/`CanTouch` off keeps parked parts out of raycasts and touch checks.
- Tracers are cosmetic: run this on each client from a replicated "shot fired" event, while hit detection stays on the server.

answer:
Allocate once, mutate in place: one shared RaycastParams, bullet state stored in parallel arrays (no per-bullet table per frame), and swap-remove for dead bullets so no new list is built. The loop then creates nothing except the Vector3 values the math needs.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.BulletSim
export type Sim = {
	count: number,
	positions: { Vector3 },
	velocities: { Vector3 },
	ages: { number },
	owners: { Player | false },
	params: RaycastParams,
}

local GRAVITY = Vector3.new(0, -workspace.Gravity * 0.25, 0)
local MAX_AGE = 3

local BulletSim = {}

function BulletSim.new(ignore: { Instance }): Sim
	local params = RaycastParams.new() -- one params object, reused for every ray
	params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
	params.FilterDescendantsInstances = ignore
	return { count = 0, positions = {}, velocities = {}, ages = {}, owners = {}, params = params }
end

function BulletSim.spawn(sim: Sim, origin: Vector3, velocity: Vector3, owner: Player?): ()
	local i = sim.count + 1
	sim.count = i
	sim.positions[i] = origin
	sim.velocities[i] = velocity
	sim.ages[i] = 0
	sim.owners[i] = owner or false
end

local function removeAt(sim: Sim, i: number)
	local last = sim.count
	sim.positions[i] = sim.positions[last]
	sim.velocities[i] = sim.velocities[last]
	sim.ages[i] = sim.ages[last]
	sim.owners[i] = sim.owners[last]
	sim.positions[last] = nil
	sim.velocities[last] = nil
	sim.ages[last] = nil
	sim.owners[last] = nil
	sim.count = last - 1
end

function BulletSim.step(sim: Sim, dt: number, onHit: (owner: Player | false, result: RaycastResult) -> ()): ()
	local i = 1
	while i <= sim.count do
		local velocity = sim.velocities[i] + GRAVITY * dt
		local displacement = velocity * dt
		local result = workspace:Raycast(sim.positions[i], displacement, sim.params)
		sim.ages[i] += dt
		if result then
			onHit(sim.owners[i], result)
			removeAt(sim, i) -- the last bullet moved into slot i; do not advance
		elseif sim.ages[i] > MAX_AGE then
			removeAt(sim, i)
		else
			sim.positions[i] += displacement
			sim.velocities[i] = velocity
			i += 1
		end
	end
end

return BulletSim
```

- Swap-remove is O(1) and allocates nothing; bullet order does not matter, so moving the last bullet into the gap is safe as long as the loop re-checks slot `i`.
- Parallel arrays stay the same tables for the whole session; with a table per bullet per frame, 300 bullets at 60 Hz is 18,000 garbage tables a second.
- Measure with the MicroProfiler before and after; if raycasts dominate, the next step is fewer rays (longer steps at lower rates), not more micro-optimisation.

answer:
Use a `SharedTable` registered under a name in `SharedTableRegistry`: every Actor gets the same table, and `SharedTable.increment` is atomic, so parallel writers never lose updates. A serial script drains it once per interval with `SharedTable.update`, which reads and removes each key atomically, so increments that land during the drain are kept for the next round.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.ThreatMap (required by the worker Actors and by the director)
local SharedTableRegistry = game:GetService("SharedTableRegistry")

local TABLE_NAME = "ThreatMap"

local ThreatMap = {}

function ThreatMap.shared(): SharedTable
	return SharedTableRegistry:GetSharedTable(TABLE_NAME)
end

-- Safe to call from any Actor, including in the parallel phase.
function ThreatMap.add(st: SharedTable, zone: string, amount: number): ()
	if amount ~= amount or amount <= 0 then
		return
	end
	SharedTable.increment(st, zone, amount)
end

-- Serial phase: returns the accumulated threat per zone and resets those entries.
function ThreatMap.drain(st: SharedTable): { [string]: number }
	local out: { [string]: number } = {}
	local zones: { string } = {}
	for zone in st do -- collect keys first; do not modify a table while iterating it
		table.insert(zones, zone)
	end
	for _, zone in zones do
		SharedTable.update(st, zone, function(value: number?): number?
			out[zone] = value or 0
			return nil -- removing the key resets that zone
		end)
	end
	return out
end

return ThreatMap
```

```lua
--!strict
-- Script inside each worker Actor: scans its share of NPCs in parallel
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local ThreatMap = require(game:GetService("ServerScriptService").ThreatMap)

local actor = script:GetActor()
local workerIndex = actor:GetAttribute("WorkerIndex") :: number
local workerCount = actor:GetAttribute("WorkerCount") :: number
local st = ThreatMap.shared()

RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel(function()
	for i, npc in CollectionService:GetTagged("Hostile") do
		if i % workerCount == workerIndex then
			local zone = npc:GetAttribute("Zone")
			if type(zone) == "string" then
				ThreatMap.add(st, zone, 1)
			end
		end
	end
end)
```

- Reading instances and attributes is allowed in the parallel phase; `SharedTable` writes are allowed too, which is what makes this pattern cheaper than messaging.
- The director (a normal Script) calls `ThreatMap.drain(ThreatMap.shared())` every second or so and acts on the totals in the serial phase.
- SharedTables hold plain values (numbers, strings, booleans, other SharedTables); store instance references as ids or names.

answer:
Time-slice it: process items until a per-frame budget (say 2 ms) is used, then yield to the next frame and continue where you stopped. The total work is unchanged, but no single frame pays for all of it.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.TimeSliced
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local TimeSliced = {}

-- Calls work(item) for every element, spending at most budgetSeconds per frame.
-- Yields between frames; returns the number of frames it took.
function TimeSliced.forEach<T>(list: { T }, budgetSeconds: number, work: (T) -> ()): number
	local frames = 1
	local frameStart = os.clock()
	for i = 1, #list do
		work(list[i])
		if os.clock() - frameStart >= budgetSeconds and i < #list then
			RunService.Heartbeat:Wait()
			frames += 1
			frameStart = os.clock()
		end
	end
	return frames
end

return TimeSliced
```

```lua
--!strict
-- Script: ServerScriptService.ValueRecalc
local ServerScriptService = game:GetService("ServerScriptService")
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local TimeSliced = require(ServerScriptService.TimeSliced)

local BUDGET = 0.002

while true do
	local totals: { [number]: number } = {}
	local placed = CollectionService:GetTagged("Placed")
	TimeSliced.forEach(placed, BUDGET, function(model: Instance)
		local owner = model:GetAttribute("OwnerId")
		local value = model:GetAttribute("Value")
		if type(owner) == "number" and type(value) == "number" then
			totals[owner] = (totals[owner] or 0) + value
		end
	end)
	for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
		player:SetAttribute("PlacedValue", totals[player.UserId] or 0)
	end
	task.wait(60)
end
```

- The list is snapshotted (`GetTagged` returns a new array), so objects added or removed mid-pass do not break the loop; an object destroyed before its turn just reads nil attributes and is skipped.
- 2 ms is a good default on a 16.7 ms frame; raise it for work players wait on, lower it if other systems are already heavy.
- Results are only consistent at the end of the pass, so publish them (leaderboard, attributes) after `forEach` returns, not item by item.

answer:
A generic min-heap stored in an array with parallel priorities: `push` sifts up, `pop` moves the last element to the root and sifts down, both O(log n). The scheduler then pops only while the earliest event is due.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.MinHeap
export type MinHeap<T> = { items: { T }, priorities: { number } }

local MinHeap = {}

function MinHeap.new<T>(): MinHeap<T>
	return { items = {}, priorities = {} }
end

local function swap<T>(heap: MinHeap<T>, i: number, j: number)
	heap.items[i], heap.items[j] = heap.items[j], heap.items[i]
	heap.priorities[i], heap.priorities[j] = heap.priorities[j], heap.priorities[i]
end

function MinHeap.push<T>(heap: MinHeap<T>, item: T, priority: number): ()
	local i = #heap.items + 1
	heap.items[i] = item
	heap.priorities[i] = priority
	while i > 1 do
		local parent = i // 2
		if heap.priorities[parent] <= heap.priorities[i] then
			break
		end
		swap(heap, i, parent)
		i = parent
	end
end

function MinHeap.peek<T>(heap: MinHeap<T>): (T?, number?)
	return heap.items[1], heap.priorities[1]
end

function MinHeap.pop<T>(heap: MinHeap<T>): (T?, number?)
	local n = #heap.items
	if n == 0 then
		return nil, nil
	end
	local top, topPriority = heap.items[1], heap.priorities[1]
	swap(heap, 1, n)
	heap.items[n] = nil
	heap.priorities[n] = nil
	n -= 1
	local i = 1
	while i * 2 <= n do
		local child = i * 2
		if child + 1 <= n and heap.priorities[child + 1] < heap.priorities[child] then
			child += 1
		end
		if heap.priorities[i] <= heap.priorities[child] then
			break
		end
		swap(heap, i, child)
		i = child
	end
	return top, topPriority
end

function MinHeap.size<T>(heap: MinHeap<T>): number
	return #heap.items
end

-- Runs every callback whose due time is <= now, earliest first. Returns how many ran.
function MinHeap.runDue(heap: MinHeap<() -> ()>, now: number): number
	local ran = 0
	local _, due = MinHeap.peek(heap)
	while due ~= nil and due <= now do
		local callback = MinHeap.pop(heap)
		if callback then
			task.spawn(callback)
			ran += 1
		end
		_, due = MinHeap.peek(heap)
	end
	return ran
end

return MinHeap
```

- Scheduler loop: `MinHeap.push(timers, function() growCrop(plot) end, os.clock() + 30)` and once per Heartbeat `MinHeap.runDue(timers, os.clock())`; a frame with nothing due costs one peek.
- Items and priorities live in parallel arrays, so the heap allocates no wrapper table per entry.
- Equal priorities come out in an unspecified order; add a sequence number as a tie-break if order matters.

I want a priority queue keyed by due time so I only touch the ones that are actually due. Can you write a generic binary heap and show it used as a scheduler?

answer:
Wrap `pcall` in a function that returns a tagged `Result<T>`: either `{ ok: true, value: T }` or `{ ok: false, err: string }`. Checking `result.ok` refines the union, so the value is only reachable on the success branch.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ReplicatedStorage.Result
export type Result<T> = { ok: true, value: T } | { ok: false, err: string }

local Result = {}

function Result.try<T, A...>(fn: (A...) -> T, ...: A...): Result<T>
	local ok, valueOrErr = pcall(fn, ...)
	if ok then
		return { ok = true, value = valueOrErr }
	end
	return { ok = false, err = tostring(valueOrErr) }
end

function Result.unwrapOr<T>(result: Result<T>, fallback: T): T
	if result.ok then
		return result.value
	end
	return fallback
end

function Result.map<T, U>(result: Result<T>, fn: (T) -> U): Result<U>
	if result.ok then
		return Result.try(fn, result.value)
	end
	return result
end

return Result
```

- Usage: `local r = Result.try(store.GetAsync, store, key)`; `if r.ok then use(r.value) else warn(r.err) end`. Writing `r.value` without the check is a type error.
- `map` chains a transformation and passes failures through untouched, so a sequence of steps needs one error check at the end.
- `tostring(valueOrErr)` normalises errors thrown as tables or Instances into a string the caller can log.

answer:
Call the function in `pcall`; on failure wait `base * 2^(attempt-1)` seconds capped at a maximum, with random jitter so many servers that failed together do not retry in lockstep. A `shouldRetry` predicate lets permanent errors fail fast.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.Retry
export type Options = {
	attempts: number?,
	baseDelay: number?,
	maxDelay: number?,
	shouldRetry: ((err: string) -> boolean)?,
	rng: Random?,
}

local Retry = {}

function Retry.backoffDelay(attempt: number, baseDelay: number, maxDelay: number, rng: Random): number
	local ceiling = math.min(maxDelay, baseDelay * 2 ^ (attempt - 1))
	-- jitter: anywhere between half and all of the ceiling
	local roll: number = rng:NextNumber()
	return ceiling * (0.5 + 0.5 * roll)
end

function Retry.call<T>(fn: () -> T, options: Options?): (boolean, T | string)
	local opts: Options = options or {}
	local attempts = opts.attempts or 4
	local baseDelay = opts.baseDelay or 0.5
	local maxDelay = opts.maxDelay or 8
	local rng = opts.rng or Random.new()
	local lastErr = "no attempts made"
	for attempt = 1, attempts do
		local ok, result = pcall(fn)
		if ok then
			return true, result
		end
		lastErr = tostring(result)
		if opts.shouldRetry and not opts.shouldRetry(lastErr) then
			break
		end
		if attempt < attempts then
			task.wait(Retry.backoffDelay(attempt, baseDelay, maxDelay, rng))
		end
	end
	return false, lastErr
end

return Retry
```

- Usage: `local ok, err = Retry.call(function() BadgeService:AwardBadge(userId, badgeId) end, { attempts = 3 })`; log `err` when `ok` is false.
- Jitter matters after a service outage: without it, every server that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment again.
- Pass `shouldRetry = function(e) return not string.find(e, "not found", 1, true) end` style predicates for errors that will never succeed. The helper yields, so call it from a thread that may wait, not from inside a callback that must return immediately.
request: I want one generic helper to retry flaky async calls (badge awards, HTTP to our own backend, MemoryStore reads). It should use exponential backoff, not hammer the service, and let me say which errors are not worth retrying. What does a good one look like?

answer:
A fixed-capacity ring buffer: writes overwrite the oldest slot, so memory stays constant and nothing shifts. Store `(time, position)` pairs and answer "where at time t" by walking back from the newest sample and interpolating between the two samples around `t`.

```lua
--!strict
-- ModuleScript: ServerScriptService.PositionHistory
export type History = {
	capacity: number,
	count: number,
	head: number, -- index of the newest sample
	times: { number },
	positions: { Vector3 },
}

local PositionHistory = {}

function PositionHistory.new(capacity: number): History
	assert(capacity >= 2, "need room for at least two samples")
	return { capacity = capacity, count = 0, head = 0, times = {}, positions = {} }
end

function PositionHistory.push(h: History, time: number, position: Vector3): ()
	h.head = h.head % h.capacity + 1
	h.times[h.head] = time
	h.positions[h.head] = position
	h.count = math.min(h.count + 1, h.capacity)
end

-- i = 0 is the newest sample, i = count - 1 the oldest
local function slot(h: History, i: number): number
	return (h.head - 1 - i) % h.capacity + 1
end

function PositionHistory.at(h: History, time: number): Vector3?
	if h.count == 0 then
		return nil
	end
	local newest = slot(h, 0)
	if time >= h.times[newest] then
		return h.positions[newest]
	end
	for i = 1, h.count - 1 do
		local older, newer = slot(h, i), slot(h, i - 1)
		local t0, t1 = h.times[older], h.times[newer]
		if time >= t0 then
			local alpha = if t1 > t0 then (time - t0) / (t1 - t0) else 0
			return h.positions[older]:Lerp(h.positions[newer], alpha)
		end
	end
	return nil -- older than anything we kept
end

return PositionHistory
```

- At 60 samples per second, `PositionHistory.new(60)` holds one second per player; size it from the oldest rewind you allow, and reject hit claims older than that (the `nil` return).
- Parallel `times`/`positions` arrays mean a push allocates nothing new after the buffer fills.
- Record from the server's Heartbeat with `os.clock()` and rewind to `os.clock() - player:GetNetworkPing()`; never take the time to rewind to from the client.
